title: When two changes collide
objectives: Resolve a merge conflict by hand
Read conflict markers and tell which half came from which branch

screens.prose: Both branches changed the same line of params.py, in different ways. You are on main and run `git merge experiment`.
screens.question: Which lookback should the merged file have?

options.text: git cannot know, so it stops and asks you
60, from the newer commit
options.why: You expected the latest change to win. git never judges by time; either value could be the one you want.

options.text: 30, from the branch you are on
options.why: Being on main gives main no priority. Both changes are real edits to the same line.

options.text: 20, the value before either change
options.why: That would throw away both edits. git keeps work; it does not undo it.

hints.text: Is there a rule that could tell which edit is right?
Both branches rewrote this line, each in its own way.
Each value is a deliberate edit. Only a person can decide, so git stops and asks.

feedback.correct: Two edits to one line: git stops and leaves the choice to you.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether any rule could pick the right value.

explain.text: Line 2 was edited on both branches, so git has two answers and no way to choose. It stops the merge and marks the clash in the file. Lines 1 and 3 changed on neither branch, so they cause no trouble.

screens.prose: git printed `CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in params.py` and stopped. You open the file. You wrote four of these lines; git wrote the rest itself.
screens.question: Tap the lines git wrote itself.

hints.text: Which lines are not Python at all?
This line is a row of seven less-than signs and a name.
git wrote three lines: one of <, one of = and one of >.

feedback.correct: The three marker lines came from git.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick only the lines that could not be in a Python file.

byKey.took-values: The two lookback lines are real code: main's version and experiment's. git only wrote the three marker lines around them.
byKey.r2c0: lookback = 30 is main's line, which you wrote earlier. git only wrote the markers.
byKey.r4c0: lookback = 60 is experiment's line, which you wrote earlier. git only wrote the markers.
byKey.r0c0: The ticker line merged cleanly. It is ordinary code.
byKey.r6c0: The cost line merged cleanly. It is ordinary code.
byKey.r1c0: Look for every line made of repeated symbols: there are three.

explain.text: git wrote three **conflict markers** around the clash. Everything else is code you wrote. The markers fence off the two versions of line 2.

screens.prose: The markers split the clash in two. HEAD is the branch you are on, and the last marker names the branch you are merging in.
screens.question: Tap the line that came from experiment.

hints.text: Which marker names experiment?
This marker names experiment. Its half is just above it.
The half between ======= and >>>>>>> experiment is experiment's version.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the half that ends at the marker naming experiment.

byKey.ours: lookback = 30 sits under <<<<<<< HEAD. HEAD is main, the branch you are on, so that is main's line.
byKey.r5c0: That is the marker itself. Tap the code line inside experiment's half.
byKey.r3c0: That is the divider between the halves. Tap a code line.

explain.text: Between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` is **ours**, main's version. Between `=======` and `>>>>>>> experiment` is **theirs**. Resolving means rewriting this block as the code you actually want.

screens.prose: Your tests showed the 60-day lookback works better. Build the finished params.py from these lines. Leave out every line that should not be in it.
screens.question: Place the lines of the finished file in order, top to bottom.

hints.text: Which lines are Python you want, and which are git's notes to you?
These three markers must all go.
Keep the ticker, then lookback = 60, then the cost line. Drop main's lookback and every marker.

feedback.correct: Three lines of plain Python, with no markers left.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the ticker, the lookback you chose and the cost line, in file order.

byKey.m1: You kept a conflict marker. Python cannot run a file containing <<<<<<<, so delete every marker line.
byKey.sep: You kept the ======= divider. It is a git note, not code, so delete it.
byKey.m3: You kept a conflict marker. Python cannot run a file containing >>>>>>>, so delete every marker line.
byKey.l30: You kept main's lookback. You chose 60, so lookback = 30 goes.
byKey.t6: The cost line comes last, after the lookback, as in the original file.

explain.text: You kept the clean lines and the version you chose, and deleted the three markers. A finished file must contain no `<<<<<<<`, `=======` or `>>>>>>>` lines. Choosing 60 was your decision; git only asked.

screens.prose: The file is fixed in your editor, but git does not know yet. `git status` still lists params.py under Unmerged paths as both modified.
screens.question: Put the steps that finish the merge in order.

lines.text: Delete the markers and save params.py
`python backtest.py`, to check the file runs
`git commit`, which makes the merge commit

hints.text: How does git learn that a file is resolved?
Fix the file and check it runs. `git add` tells git it is resolved; `git commit` makes the merge commit.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. git only counts the file as resolved once you add it, and the commit comes last.

byKey.add: You added the file before fixing it, so the markers would go into the commit.
byKey.commit: You committed before adding. git refuses while a file is still unmerged.
byKey.check: Check the file after you edit it and before you add it, so a broken file never gets committed.

explain.text: `git add params.py` is how you tell git the conflict is resolved. `git commit` then makes the merge commit, with two parents as usual. Running the backtest first catches a stray marker before it is committed.

screens.prose: Another merge. This time main changed line 1 and experiment changed line 3. Line 2 was left alone by both.
screens.question: What does `git merge experiment` do?

options.text: Merges cleanly: ticker QQQ and cost_bps 8
Stops with a conflict, because both changed params.py
options.why: git compares lines, not whole files. Edits to separate lines combine without asking.

options.text: Keeps main's file and drops experiment's change
options.why: Nothing clashes, so git keeps both edits.

options.text: Keeps experiment's file, so the ticker goes back to SPY
options.why: Nothing clashes, so git keeps both edits.

hints.text: Did both branches change the same line?
main changed only line 1, and experiment only line 3.
Separate lines, with an untouched line between them: git takes each change from the branch that made it.

feedback.correct: Separate lines merge cleanly: you get both edits.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the two edits touch the same lines.

explain.text: Each line was changed on at most one branch, so git takes each edit from where it was made. The result has ticker QQQ and cost_bps 8, with no conflict. Edits to touching lines, with nothing unchanged between them, do clash.

screens.prose: Two branches each added a new signal to the same list. You want both signals in the backtest.
screens.question: Place the lines of the finished signals.py in order.

hints.text: Does keeping one signal mean losing the other?
Each half holds one new signal, and you want both.
Open the list, keep trend, keep both carry and value, then close it. Drop the three markers.

feedback.correct: All three signals, and no markers.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep every signal you want, and none of the markers.

byKey.close: You closed the list after one new signal. A conflict does not mean one side must lose: keep both carry and value.
byKey.m1: You kept a conflict marker. Delete all three marker lines.
byKey.sep: You kept the ======= divider. Delete all three marker lines.
byKey.m3: You kept a conflict marker. Delete all three marker lines.
byKey.trend: trend was in the list before the split. Keep it, right after the opening line.

explain.text: You kept both halves, because each added something you want. A conflict only means git will not choose for you. The answer can be ours, theirs, both, or a new line written by hand.

screens.prose:
Every conflict has this shape:

```sh
<<<<<<< HEAD
your branch's lines
=======
the other branch's lines
>>>>>>> other-branch
```

Rewrite the block as the code you want, delete the markers, then `git add` and `git commit`.
screens.question: When does git count the conflict as resolved?

options.text: When you `git add` the fixed file
As soon as you save the file
options.why: git does not watch your editor. Saving changes the folder; `git add` tells git.

options.text: When you delete one side's lines
options.why: git does not read your edits until you add the file.

options.text: Only after `git merge --abort`
options.why: `--abort` cancels the merge and puts main back as it was. Nothing is resolved.

hints.text: Which command did `git status` tell you to use?
git status said: use git add to mark resolution.

feedback.correct: `git add` marks the file resolved; `git commit` finishes the merge.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look back at what `git status` suggested.

explain.text: `git add` records the fixed file and marks it resolved. When no unmerged files are left, `git commit` makes the merge commit. If you want to start again, `git merge --abort` returns to before the merge.

screens.prose: Before the split, config.yaml said lookback: 20 and cost_bps: 5. On main, a colleague raised costs to 8 bps after checking real fills. On vol-signal you set lookback to 60. The two lines touch, so git reports one conflict.
screens.question: Place the lines of the correct config.yaml in order.

hints.text: Compare each half with the file before the split. Which line did each side actually change?
main's half changed cost_bps; your half changed lookback.
Take lookback: 60 from your branch and cost_bps: 8 from main. Keep ticker and start, and drop the markers.

feedback.correct: lookback 60 from your branch, costs of 8 bps from main.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take each side's real change, and nothing else.

byKey.lb20: You kept main's half whole. lookback: 20 undoes your own change; take lookback from your branch.
byKey.c5: You kept your branch's half whole. cost_bps: 5 silently undoes your colleague's fix to 8 bps.
byKey.m1: You kept a conflict marker. Delete all three.
byKey.sep: You kept the ======= divider. Delete all three markers.
byKey.m3: You kept a conflict marker. Delete all three.
byKey.start: start: 2015-01-01 is the last line, after both settings.

explain.text: Each half repeats one line it never changed. Comparing with the file before the split shows the real edits: lookback on your branch, cost_bps on main. Keeping either half whole would quietly undo the other person's work, and flatter or break the backtest.

ideas: git stops with a conflict when both branches changed the same or touching lines. Edits to separate lines merge cleanly.
Between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` is your branch; between `=======` and `>>>>>>> name` is the other one.
Rewrite the block as the code you want, delete every marker, then `git add` the file and `git commit`.

formula.name: Finish a conflicted merge
formula.note: Compare each half with the file before the split to see what each side really changed.

summary.trap: A conflict does not mean one side must win. Keeping a whole half can silently undo the other branch's change.

quiz.prose:
You are on main and merge the branch fees. You see:

```sh
<<<<<<< HEAD
fee = 0.0005
=======
fee = 0.0010
>>>>>>> fees
```
quiz.question: Which value came from main?

options.why: That is under the divider, in the half ending >>>>>>> fees. It came from fees.

options.text: Neither: main's value is not shown
options.why: Both versions are shown. HEAD's half is main's.

feedback.correct: The half under <<<<<<< HEAD is the branch you are on: main.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which marker is HEAD?

explain.text: HEAD is main, the branch you are on. Its half runs from `<<<<<<< HEAD` to `=======`. So main has 0.0005 and fees has 0.0010.

quiz.prose: A merge leaves backtest.py with markers in it. Searching for `=======` finds 2 lines, and each conflict has 3 marker lines.
quiz.question: How many conflicts must you resolve in backtest.py?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many dividers does one conflict have?

byKey.markers: You counted marker lines. Each conflict has three of them, so 6 lines is 2 conflicts.
byKey.halves: You counted halves. Each conflict has two halves, so 4 halves is 2 conflicts.

explain.text: Each conflict has exactly one `=======` divider. Two dividers means two conflicts, with 6 marker lines in all. Every one must go before you `git add` the file.

quiz.prose:
To be safe, you resolve a conflict by keeping both versions:

```sh
lookback = 30
lookback = 60
```
quiz.question: What lookback does the backtest now use?

options.text: 60, silently: the second line overwrites the first
None: Python stops with an error
options.why: Assigning a name twice is legal Python. Nothing warns you.

options.text: 30, the first one
options.why: Python runs top to bottom, so the later line wins.

options.text: Both: it runs once with each
options.why: A name holds one value at a time. The second line replaces the first.

feedback.correct: The later line wins, and nothing warns you.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Python runs the lines top to bottom.

explain.text: Keeping both lines is not safe here. Python sets lookback to 30, then to 60. Two values for one setting means you must choose one.

quiz.prose: You deleted the markers in params.py and saved it. `git status` still shows `both modified: params.py`.
quiz.question: What do you run next?

options.text: `git add params.py`
`git merge experiment` again
options.why: A merge is already in progress. Running it again does not finish it.

options.text: `git merge --abort`
options.why: That throws away the merge and your resolution.

options.text: `git commit` straight away
options.why: git refuses to commit while a file is still unmerged. Add it first.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. How does git learn that you fixed the file?

explain.text: Saving changes the folder, not git's record. `git add params.py` marks it resolved. Then `git commit` makes the merge commit.
